newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao named in several legal cases.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao named in several legal cases.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, exempted from having to make an unprecedented court appearance on Monday, has been named in several corruption cases.
Following are summaries of the three cases in which Rao, who served as prime minister from mid-1991 until last May, has either been charged or is under investigation.
CHEATING SCANDAL
An Indian expatriate businessman, Lakhubhai Pathak, alleges Rao and a Hindu guru named Chandraswami conspired to cheat him of $100,000 in 1983.

Pathak claims he paid money to Chandraswami in an unsuccessful attempt to win a state newsprint contract after Rao, then foreign minister, assured him at a meeting in a New York hotel that his "work will be done".

In July, a Delhi judge summoned Rao to appear in court to face charges. Rao lost two appeals to have the summons overturned. Judge Ajit Bharihoke upheld the summons on September 21 and ordered Rao to appear in his court on September 30 to face charges.
The former prime minister, who quit as Congress party chief hours after the judge's ruling on September 21, was later denied legal protection against arrest.

On Monday September 30 the Supreme Court exempted Rao from having to appear in court. But the court could still charge Rao with criminal conspiracy to cheat, which carries a maximum penalty of seven years in jail.
If arrested and denied bail, he could be put under judicial custody, probably at Tihar jail, or police custody, perhaps in his home, pending trial.
The two other co-accused, Chandraswami and his personal assistant, are both under custody in Tihar, Asia's biggest prison with some 10,000 inmates.
Rao has said he is innocent and has denied he was in New York on the dates mentioned by Pathak.
ST KITTS

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's federal police, charged Rao and three others on September 26 in a forgery case involving an alleged attempt in 1989 to tarnish the reputation of V.P. Singh, an opposition leader who later became prime minister.
The case involves the alleged falsification of bank documents to show that Singh's son, Ajeya Singh, had a secret bank account with large amounts of money on the Caribbean island of St Kitts.
At the time V.P. Singh, who had left the ruling Congress party for the opposition, was spearheading an anti-corruption campaign against the government.

V.P. Singh was appointed prime minister at the end of 1989 after Congress lost general polls. Authorities later cleared Ajeya Singh of allegations that he had violated foreign exchange and anti-corruption laws.

A CBI statement last week said its investigation "revealed that the accused persons, in conspiring with each other, fabricated false evidence with the intent and knowledge to...harm their (V.P. Singh and Ajeya Singh) reputation in the eyes of the public".

The federal police agency said the four accused were charged with criminal conspiracy, forgery, giving false evidence and using forged documents. It did not say what possible penalties the charges carried.
Rao was not believed to have commented publicly on the case, which was due to be taken up by a Delhi court on October 1.
VOTE-BUYING SCANDAL
Lawmakers of the regional Jharkand Mukti Morcha party said they were paid $100,000 to vote against a 1993 no-confidence motion which Rao's Congress-led government survived by a wafer-thin margin.
Earlier this year the CBI filed a case accusing Rao and other Congress leaders of buying the votes. They have denied any wrongdoing. The case is still under investigation.
